content.thinking:
I'm planning out a treasure hoard design, League of Legends style, with a coin mound base, an open chest glowing with gold, a crown, goblets, and glowing gems, sized roughly 1.2 meters wide and 0.8 meters tall. I'm thinking through how to structure the scene as plain objects using the builder API.

I'm deciding to set up a root joint at the origin and a separate hinge joint for the chest lid, making sure every part explicitly specifies which bone it attaches to so geometry doesn't get misassigned to the wrong joint, and I'm planning a small helper function to simplify placing parts with a default color, position, and bone.

Now I'm sketching the actual chest geometry: using cel-shaded paints for the color palette, choosing primitive shapes like boxes and cylinders for the body and lid, and figuring out how to build the lid as a curved or paneled shape that opens on a back hinge at roughly 110 degrees.

Working out the hinge joint's exact position at the back-top edge of the chest body, then defining the lid as a half-cylinder shape rotated to align its axis with the box's width.

Since the cut plane leaves the interior visible from certain angles, I'll add a dark wood underside plank beneath the lid and an inner lining box to hide the gap, keeping things low-poly with flat shading. For the chest body, I'm planning a wood paint with vertical plank lines simulated via a custom paint function based on position along the x-axis.

For the interior, I'll add a heap of gold sticking up above the chest's top face — a squashed sphere scaled flat and wide to look like a coin pile, positioned just above the box's rim so it reads as treasure spilling out, plus scattered coins and gems on top.

Writing paint shaders...

Now I'm adding metal bands with rivets, a gold lock plate with keyhole decal, and considering a teal glowing rune accent to give it that hextech-style look.

Next I'm placing a tilted crown on the coin pile, building its band via a lathe shape and planning gem-tipped spikes to add on top.

Writing group transform helper code...

Verifying the edges don't cross and the axis closure works cleanly, then I'll add a gem band around the goblet bowl using small embedded octahedrons, paint it gold, and scale the whole profile up by a factor for better readability via a helper function.

Now I'm thinking through tipping the goblet onto its side by rotating the group roughly 80° about the Z axis, then figuring out how to position it resting on its rim and foot so it sits properly on the floor among scattered coins. I'll also add a low, dark purple-blue stone floor disc beneath everything to ground the scene.

For the floor, I'm defining it as a thin disc from y=0 to y=0.04, with all objects resting at that top surface. The coin pile becomes a squashed gold mound in front of the chest, and I'm planning to scatter individual coin discs across its surface -- but since hundreds of separate coin parts would blow past the part limit, I need to merge their geometry by color rather than creating each as its own stick.

Instead I'll build each coin's transform manually from the scatter hit's position and normal, orient it with a quaternion plus a random spin, then merge all the coin geometries per color group (gold, goldlight, silver) into single parts using mergeGeometries, since the cylinder's indexed attributes merge cleanly. I'll use cel-shaded painting on the merged coin parts for a better look within the color budget, driving the shading pattern from UV coordinates.

For the mound, instead of a full sphere I'll use a hemisphere (thetaLength = π/2) so it doesn't dip below the floor, scaling it to a flattened dome shape and filtering scatter hits to only the upward-facing normals so coins only land on top. I'm planning multiple mounds, starting with a main one in front.

Then I add two smaller side mounds plus some loose coins spilled flat on the floor, with coin counts roughly 140 for the main pile and 60 for each smaller one, keeping triangle counts low by using simple 8-sided cylinder coins.

For some standout detail, I'm adding a handful of hero coins leaning against the mound with an embossed star emblem, built from a gold cylinder plus a circle decal plane on the face to avoid texture bleeding onto the sides.

Then I'm scattering 40-50 small glowing gems around the scene in different colors—ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, topaz—each as its own flat part with its own glow material so the colors stay distinct.

I'll convert all gem geometries to non-indexed form safely with a helper, confirming they share position, normal, and uv attributes so merging works cleanly, and apply matrix transforms before combining. For hero gems, I'm planning a sapphire crystal cluster with tall hexagonal prisms and pointed tops near the chest.

Each crystal combines a hexagonal cylinder base with a cone tip, merged by color, with one cyan-glowing cluster on the left and a magenta cluster on the right at varying heights. I also want to embed a few glowing gems on the chest lid, attached separately to the lid bone so they animate correctly, before moving on to think about necklace pearls.

For the pearl necklace, I'll sweep a catmull-rom path with gold chain geometry merged with white pearl spheres, making sure to anchor it to the root bone rather than letting weight-based bone selection pick the lid joint by accident. For the goblets, I'm placing one upright on the floor and one tipped over spilling a coin trail toward +Z, and considering adding a third small chalice for variety.

Now I'm positioning a smaller third goblet standing atop the main mound, slightly sunk into its surface with a gold-and-sapphire finish. I'm also working out where to place a crown as the hero piece -- deciding between the right mound and the central mound, ultimately tilting it atop the central mound front with a scaled-up radius for prominence, while keeping goblet C off to the side on the left mound.

Shaping the overflowing coin sack outline...

Adding a flared cone collar for the sack's puffy neck fan, plus gold coins spilling out as a small dome sphere near the top opening.

Now I'm checking the layout math — positioning the chest and sack mound along x/z coordinates to make sure the mound overlaps the chest front just enough to look like it's leaning against it, rather than floating separately.

Placing props around the oval floor: an upright goblet and coin sack to the right, a tipped goblet with spilled coins trailing left, a third goblet on the left mound top, and a small gold key with ring, rod, and teeth near the front. Now sketching the bumpy stone floor as a wide cylinder base.

I need the ring strokes thick enough to render clearly at this resolution, so I'll bump the plane slightly higher to avoid z-fighting with the floor. Now I'm working out the chest's total height with the lid open, accounting for the hinge rotation and lid depth to see how far it swings up.

With the lid tilted back roughly 75°, the chest ends up around 0.82m tall, which feels reasonable against a 2.5 diameter floor, though I'll shrink the floor radius down to 1.15 to keep proportions tighter for the diorama. Now I'm laying out the iron bands on the chest body and the curved bands on the lid, plus planning small rivet spheres along the bands.

I'm adding corner brackets as boxes at the bottom and top corners, and a lower trim steel band near the base. For the wood texture on the front and sides, I'm writing a plank pattern that creates horizontal board lines based on vertical spacing.

Still writing plank logic...

I'm checking that paint and cel compose correctly for lit coloring, confirming the needed imports from the paint module and toon kit, and planning a metallic cel-shaded look for steel using mottled tones. I'm now working out the color palette, mapping flat strings for simpler materials and paint functions like mottle for gems, runes, and gold.

Still building the palette...

Now I'm setting up the imports and module structure for the scene file, pulling in geometry utilities, path helpers, and paint/texture functions I'll need.

Setting up the build function with metadata and starting the joint hierarchy for a treasure hoard model...

Building a frame helper that converts local positions and rotations into world-space transforms using quaternions...

Still writing part helper...

For lathe shapes, I need to handle orientation differently since they aren't placed via `put` -- I'm computing an axis vector by rotating the Y axis with the quaternion derived from the rotation input, then passing that axis into the lathe helper alongside position, segments, and color.

I'm scaling the outline coordinates manually before passing them to the lathe function, and setting up a gem collection system that maps colors to geometry arrays, with a helper that builds different polyhedron shapes (octahedron, icosahedron, dodecahedron, tetrahedron) based on a kind index, position, size, rotation, and stretch factor.

I'm realizing that if I merge all gem geometries per color and apply flat shading with a single emissive color, the facets will lose their distinct shading and just look like a flat blob, so I need a different approach to preserve the faceted gem look.

Settling on an emissive strength of 0.5 so facets still shade differently under lighting while adding glow brightness. For crystal clusters, I'm now thinking through building each crystal as a merged shaft-and-tip geometry, similar to the gem construction approach.

Still writing coin placement logic...

For the mound surface, I'm adding faceted hemisphere geometry so the coin scatter normals come from flat faces, then darkening the gold paint with a mottled cel shader so coins stand out against it. For hero coins leaning on the mound, I'm positioning a rotated cylinder so its flat face points outward instead of upward.

Working out the rotation so the coin's decal plane aligns with its tilted face normal, checking how rotating around X maps the local Z axis toward Y for the correct orientation.

For the opposite face I'll mirror with the equivalent rotation, and roll orientation doesn't matter since the emblem is fairly symmetric. I'm sketching the coin texture as an SVG with a gold circle, darker stroke rings, and a star shape, rendered on a small circular plane geometry, then placing several of these hero coins scattered around the front of the main mound.

For each coin I'm working out the tilt: leaning back about 15° so the face points mostly forward and slightly upward, positioning the pivot so the bottom edge roughly touches the ground, and sorting out how the Euler rotation order affects adding a yaw component without breaking the tilt.

Working through the rotation math, I confirm the roughly 10° yaw gives a reasonable tilted axis direction, and decal placement stays consistent using the same local-to-global quaternion composition. Now I'm shifting focus to the chest itself — since all its parts sit on the bone root except lid pieces on the lid bone, I can use simple placement without extra frames, starting with the main chest body box sized and centered appropriately.

I'm adjusting dimensions so the body sits flush on the floor (bottom at y=.03) with height .35, spanning up to .38 where the hinge sits, and setting the lid cylinder radius to match. Now I'm defining the wood-colored box geometry for the body and starting on the rim frame pieces around the top edge using thin darker wood boxes.

Adding more rim boxes...

I'm adding the dark red interior lining just below the rim, then placing a gold dome hemisphere on top sized to clear the rim, followed by scattering coins and gems across its surface. For the opened-lid state I also need a matching red lining box on the underside of the lid so the interior shows correctly when rotated open on its hinge.

The lid itself is a half-cylinder (partial cylinder geometry cut along its length) positioned and rotated to sit atop the chest like a rounded lid, but I realize the open cut face creates a backface-culling problem -- viewed from below after opening, the inner surface normals face away from the camera, so the lining box meant to hide that gap might not render correctly from that angle.

I'm adjusting the lining box dimensions to .8x.012x.46 positioned closer to the cylinder's inner surface so it fully covers the opening without visible gaps at the edges. For the lid's steel trim, I'm adding small half-cylinder bands near the ends plus a front lip bar to give it a banded, reinforced look.

Now I'm considering ornamentation for the lid, like a gold rim or gem placement, calculating the exact angle and position to place a ruby near the front using trigonometry so it sits naturally on the curved surface with an outward-facing normal, and thinking through how to attach that gem to the correct bone for proper transform inheritance.

Placing lid gems...

I'm positioning a gold front lock plate on the body, then adding a dark keyhole texture plane, a small blue gem on top, and glowing rune strip textures below on the front face for extra detail.

Now I'm placing the steel reinforcement bands on either side of the body, slightly protruding, and checking their height matches the body's top surface so they don't clash with the dome or rim frames.

I'm positioning the bottom trim strip and vertical corner brackets at the four corners, then working out gold rivet positions along the front faces of the bands to add detail.

Skipping the chest feet for now, I'm moving to the body's wood plank texture and the gold dome, then sketching out the crown geometry as a lathed profile with a defined outline and positioning offset.

Still writing crown spikes...

Since octahedra are symmetric, orientation doesn't matter beyond the stretch. For the velvet cap, I'm using a lathe dome with a red velvet outline over the band region, sunk slightly into the mound base. Now I'm starting the goblet lathe function that builds the shape scaled by a given frame.

Adding stem knob and gem details...

For goblet A I'm placing a gold hemisphere dome inside to represent a mound of coins, while goblet B gets tipped over at a steep rotation angle with coins spilling out onto the floor instead of staying filled.

I'm working through the geometry so the tipped goblet actually rests believably on the floor: finding where the foot and rim touch down given the tilt angle, so the base sits near the floor level while the rim lifts up slightly from the tilt, keeping the whole thing physically plausible.

With cup center at F+.155 and tilted, the rim ends up resting right at floor level, so the cup looks naturally placed with the stem slightly raised. I'll orient it with a rotation around the vertical axis so the mouth faces +x, then figure out where the spilled coins land relative to the mound position around (-0.62, 0.02) and the main mound near (0, .34), adjusting B's position so the trail connects sensibly between them.

Now I'm scattering loose floor coins — generating around 18-24 of them along an arc, mostly lying flat with small random tilts and yaw so they look naturally strewn near the trail and around the mound. I'm also placing a key, built from a torus ring plus a cylindrical shaft and small tooth boxes positioned along the shaft, rotated and offset so it reads as a simple key shape sitting near the coins.

For the sack, I'm building it from a lathe body, a rope torus around the neck, a gold dome top, and a draped cone for the cloth opening, plus a small patch box on the front for a stitched detail -- adjusting positions so the dome and cone align without clipping into each other.

Rounding out the sack silhouette to about .29 tall, then adding a rope torus cinching it near the top. For the cliff scene I want gold and gems spilling out, so I'm planning to scatter roughly 28 gems across the mounds using surface sampling, filtering for points above y=.3 to keep them on the upper slopes.

I'm varying gem color, size, and orientation randomly, and running separate scatter passes for the main pile, left/right mounds, and the chest dome, placing each gem slightly offset from the surface normal. I'm also adding coin and gem scatter inside the chest dome itself, then working out a pearl necklace draped across the front-left of the main mound by computing points that lie exactly on the ellipsoid surface of that mound.

For the pearls, I'm snapping approximate path points onto the actual mesh surface using nearest-point lookups, offsetting slightly along the normal, then building a catmull-rom curve through those points and sweeping small pearl spheres along it as a chain, with a larger pendant gem hanging at the curve's midpoint.

I'm considering a few decorative extras — maybe a hovering glowing ruby orb or small floating diamond sparkles above the chest for accent, plus a glowing rune ring on the ground for atmosphere, and sketching out an SVG helper for drawing cyan rune strokes.

Writing rune generation code...

Adding stone geometry...

I'm scattering a handful of loose gems across the floor in a few random open spots, skipping extra decor like a skull or scepter to stay focused. I'm planning to pose the lid open last, after all lid parts and gems are built, so the rotation applies cleanly to the finished assembly, then double-checking the hinge's half-cylinder geometry.

Now I'm working through the rotation math for the lid's hinge: tracking how the top point and front lip of the lid arc move in y and z after applying a -105° rotation about the hinge axis, to make sure the open lid lands at a believable angle without clipping the chest body.

I check that the red interior lining normal flips to face the viewer correctly after rotation, confirming the hinge joint logic is sound, then move on to implementing the geometry in TypeScript, being careful to avoid unused variable errors while keeping shared constants like INK and R referenced. Setting up vector types...

Now I'm defining the plank wood-texture paint function, using a toon-shaded cel paint that samples position along the board to create a repeating grain pattern with darker seam lines, then checking how to layer additional streak noise for more natural variation.

Next I'm setting up gem batching infrastructure—creating a map to group geometries by material key, a helper to append geometries into that map, and a `gem` function that builds different polyhedron shapes (octahedron, icosahedron, dodecahedron, tetrahedron) based on a kind index, then positions and orients them using a composed transform matrix.

I'm also writing a `crystal` function that builds a cylinder shaft plus a cone tip to form crystal shapes, transforming each piece into place and adding both into the same gem batch.

Now I'm setting up coin geometry batches, defining a `coin` function that positions, rotates, and scales coin meshes grouped by color index.

Writing pile scatter logic...

I should just use a simpler type for the target parameter instead of overcomplicating it. I also need to double check that scatter's rejection of buried points only applies among target meshes, which should be fine for scattering on parts under a joint root.

Now I'm designing a mound builder helper that creates hemisphere-shaped parts from sphere geometry, and a gem-scattering function that places colored gems on mounds using filtered scatter hits, randomizing size and rotation for each gem.

I also need to think through build ordering so geometry exists before scattering reads surface normals, then merge coin batches by color at the end using geometry merging for efficiency.

Finishing up the gem batch, I'm merging each color group and applying the glow effect, checking that the painted material naming still resolves correctly after merge, and guarding against null geometries. I also need to confirm the Map iteration pattern for gemBatch works fine with the target TypeScript config.

Now I'm writing the goblet function's lathe profile, checking that the outline points don't cross themselves—tracing through each segment of the shape to verify no self-intersections occur, particularly around the narrow stem and bowl transition points.

Checking the dome fits: a sphere radius .058 sitting at y .24 clears the rim height .262, with its top reaching .286, so it pokes above comfortably without clipping the cup walls. Now I'm positioning a ring of six gems spaced 60 degrees apart around the circumference.

For the torus rim and foot details, I'm adding a tube-shaped band at the rim and a smaller foot torus at the base, plus a lathe helper function that builds rotationally-symmetric shapes from a 2D profile curve along a chosen axis.

Now I'm sketching out the crown's lathe profiles for the band and the velvet cap, checking that the vertex coordinates connect cleanly without overlapping surfaces that would cause z-fighting at the inner wall.

Working out the spikes next, alternating tall and short cones arranged radially around the crown using four-sided diamond-faced geometry for the tall ones and a similar shape for the short ones.

Tipping each tall spike with a gemstone and each short spike with a pearl, merging the pearls into a shared geometry batch for efficiency. Adding a band of cycling gems offset between the spikes, and finishing with trim torus rings at the top and bottom edges of the crown.

Now I'm checking the TypeScript types for the part definitions, making sure scale and quaternion props line up, and planning glow effects for the lid gems and sparkle details. For the floor coins, I'm scattering them in a ring outside the mound radius using randomized angle and distance so they don't overlap the central piles.

Placing a trail of coins leading toward point B, tilting each one randomly for a natural scattered look, then adding six gems around that same ring and sparkles positioned near the chest and crown at a modest height to avoid making the pile look too tall. Now I'm working out coordinates for a pearl necklace draped nearby.

Still working out hero coin placement against the mound edge, but it conflicts with the key position, so I'm nudging the key further up to around (0.05,.95) to keep everything within the floor radius.

Checking right-mound hero coins near (.55,.3) against the edge at .26, settling on four coin spots total. Then I'm testing Goblet A's position against a hero coin -- they're too close given their radii, so I'm shifting the coin to (.22,.80) and adjusting the key again, while confirming the sack placement at (.88,.28) stays clear of the goblet and mound.

Now I'm reworking the sack position since it overlaps the mound edge, moving it to (.9,.42), and checking that it stays far enough from the nearby hero coin and goblet. Shifting to the left mound, I'm placing Goblet C on top accounting for sunken base height, then working out where the left chest and Goblet B sit relative to the mound, checking distances so B's body doesn't collide with the mound radius.

Checking the coin trail near the main mound's front edge, I confirm the overlap with the mound boundary is natural and acceptable, and verify the left chest base stays within the floor radius. I'm then adjusting the hero coin positions and nearby goblet A slightly to avoid them sitting too close to the key and other coins, nudging goblet A further out to keep spacing comfortable.

Now I'm placing the cyan crystal cluster near the left side, defining several small crystal shards with varied heights, radii, and tilts around a base point, then mirroring a similar magenta cluster on the right along with a small ruby accent cluster. I'm also compiling the gem color palette—ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, topaz—and assigning the crystal clusters their own cyan and magenta hex tones.

I'm reusing existing colors to keep the palette tight, defining the sack's burlap material with a grain texture paired with a fixed shadow tone, and now placing the lock plate's gem and metal plate geometry at specific coordinates on the chest's front face.

Positioning rivets at the plate corners, then setting up the keyhole decal as a textured plane and adding a glowing rune plane with white coloring near the top.

Finalizing the type definitions and making sure the lathe outline and vector cloning work correctly, then double-checking the local "frame" variable name doesn't clash with anything from the imported SDK.
